If the investigation finds the information to be inaccurate, the furnisher must promptly notify the consumer reporting agencies and provide any necessary corrections.

I am writing to file a formal complaint against JPMorgan Chase Bank ( Chase ) concerning its refusal to honor its stated Zero Liability Protection policy regarding unauthorized charges on my credit card. Despite providing substantial evidence of fraud, Chase has rebilled me for over {$3400.00} of clearly unauthorized transactions, in direct conflict with federal law and Chases own contractual obligations.

Chase publicly states : With Chases Zero Liability Protection you wont be held responsible for unauthorized charges made with your card or account information. I relied on this policy in good faith when I reported the unauthorized transactions. 

INITIAL AUTHORIZED PURCHASES On XX/XX/2024, I explicitly authorized a contractor to purchase : Two ( 2 ) 4x4x10 ft. posts, Two ( 2 ) bags of fast-set concrete, Spindles for a playhouse project. These purchases were made on XX/XX/2024 for {$55.00} and {$300.00}, which I approved. By XX/XX/2024, I had fully paid the contractor for completion of the playset project. 

UNAUTHORIZED USE After completing the authorized work on XX/XX/2024, the contractor retained my physical credit card instead of returning it. Beginning around XX/XX/2024, the contractor used my card for unrelated charges without my authorization. I discovered these fraudulent transactions on XX/XX/2024, promptly notified Chase well within the 60-day statutory period, and filed a police report with the XXXX, XXXX Police Department ( Report # XXXX ). 

CHASE 'S POSITION Chases denial letter states that I supposedly benefitted from these transactions and that granting the contractor temporary permission to use my card on XX/XX/2024, equates to perpetual authorization for any subsequent charges. 

MY RESPONSE The only purchases I authorized were those made on XX/XX/2024, for a total of {$360.00} ( {$55.00} + {$300.00} ). After that date, I neither authorized nor had knowledge of any further use. The contractor verbally agreed to return my card, but did not do so. The unauthorized purchases provided no benefit to me ; in fact, the contractor later admitted in writing that he used the card for other projects unrelated to my property. These facts clearly establish that any charges beyond XX/XX/2024, were unauthorized and should be covered under both federal law and Chases Zero Liability Protection. 

APPLICABLE LAWS Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ), 15 U.S.C. 1666 et seq. Under the FCBA, cardholders are protected from unauthorized charges if they report them within 60 days of the statement date on which those charges appear. I reported these transactions within this period, triggering Chases obligation to investigate and resolve the dispute properly. Regulation Z ( 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ) implements the Truth in Lending Act and obligates credit card issuers to conduct a good-faith investigation of disputed charges. Any denial of a claim must be accompanied by substantial evidence. Chases denial does not address or refute the objective evidence ( police report, text message admissions, and the clear timeline of events ). Liability Limits ( 15 U.S.C. 1643 ) Under the Truth in Lending Act, a cardholders liability for unauthorized use can not exceed {$50.00} if the cardholder promptly notifies the issuer. I have more than met this requirement. Moreover, Chase advertises a Zero Liability policy that should eliminate any cost to me if charges are unauthorized. 

EVIDENCE ATTACHED XXXX. Police Report from XXXX, InXXXX Police Department, Report # XXXX. 
2. Text Message Exchanges ( Dated XX/XX/2024 ) clearly showing the limited authorization for the XX/XX/2024 purchases. 
3. Contractors Admission ( XX/XX/2024 ). Written acknowledgment that he used my credit card for additional, non-beneficial projects. 
4. Chase 's denial of transactions in question ( XX/XX/2024 ). Their reason states that I benefitted from these transactions, which is clearly not true based on the evidence provided. 

I have acted in good faith and in accordance with all legal and contractual obligations. I reported the fraud in a timely manner, provided comprehensive evidence, and cooperated with both law enforcement and Chases investigation. Nevertheless, Chase continues to hold me responsible for charges that are clearly unauthorized. 

Given these circumstances, I request the Consumer Financial Protection Bureaus assistance in ensuring Chase fulfills its legal responsibilities. I appreciate your prompt attention to this matter and look forward to a fair resolution.

I believe it is unfair to have my financial future impacted so heavily by one mistake that happened while I was still a minor, especially when I was the victim of fraud. I am requesting that the CFPB look into this issue and urge XXXX  and the reporting bank to provide a transparent explanation and a path to resolution. My husband and I received a promotional offer for 0 % interest on balance transfers to our Chase United Mileage Plus card. We use this card for many of our daily purchases so we can accrue as many miles as possible and always paid it in full each month. We had a balance on another high interest credit card that was a little over $ XXXX we wanted to transfer that amount to the Chase United card, however were unsure how to pay our new charges, plus the amount owed for the balance transfer in order to keep the 0 % rate on that amount. Before transferring our balance in XX/XX/XXXX, we called Chase 's customer service department to ask how to handle our monthly payments so we could retain the promotional interest rate. We were told that we should pay the total amount of our new monthly charges plus the minimum payment due and and that would ensure we keep our 0 % interest rate. 
Based on this information, we decided to transfer the balance of our other card to our Chase United Mileage Plus card. On our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we noticed a small interest fee charged to our account, but because it was minimal ( {$64.00} ), just figured I made an incorrect calculation on paying off our purchases on the XX/XX/XXXX bill. On our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we noticed that we were charged {$210.00} in interest, but didn't pay our card in full that month, so figured that was how we accrued that interest. On our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we were charged interest in the amount of {$190.00} and in XX/XX/XXXX, we were charged {$180.00} despite paying our bills in full ( minus the amount transferred to the card ). I thought I must be calculating the balance to pay each month incorrectly because when I looked at the table of interest charges on the back page of our statement, the amount subject to interest fees was always higher than our purchases. So, I began paying the balance subject to the higher interest rate on the back of the statement each month plus the minimum amount due to hopefully get rid of the interest charges. 
However, on our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we were still charged {$200.00} in interest. I called Chase 's customer service department again and was told the same information that we were told before transferring the balance- pay your monthly charges and your minimum amount due and you will not be charged interest. For two additional months, we continued to try to figure out the correct amount to pay so that we would not be charged interest on our balance. Yet, on our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we were charged {$150.00} in interest and on our XX/XX/XXXX statement, we were charged {$180.00}. Frustrated and confused, I called Chase 's customer service yet again, and was finally told that having the balance transfer on our account was causing us to be charged daily interest on new charges. We couldn't believe it. We had never heard of this practice before- not from other credit card companies ( I checked our other credit card 's terms to see if this was a customary interest charge we were unaware of- it's not ) and not from Chase 's employees, either. 
I asked for a copy of our card agreement to be sent to us, which we received right away. The agreement states, " If you pay your account in full each month ( or Interest Saving Balance ) in full each billing period by the date and time due, no interest is charged on new purchases month to month. Also, we will not impose interest charges on any portion of a purchase balance you repay while that balance is subject to an interest-free period. Subject to any interest-free period for new purchases, we will begin charging interest from the date a transaction, fee, or interest charge is added to your daily balance until your account is paid in full. '' This is confusing wording because we were paying all monthly purchases charged to our account in full each month, except for the amount that was subject to an interest-free period. That led us to believe that our account would be considered to be paid in full each month and therefore not subject to any interest. Furthermore, the agreement states that daily interest will accrue if there is a balance due to an interest-free period on NEW purchases. Our balance was the result of a balance transfer, NOT new purchases, so we don't believe that our balance transfer should have subjected us to daily interest charges. 
Once we learned this information, we paid off the remaining balance ( new charges plus the remaining balance on the balance transfer ) in XX/XX/XXXX. We didn't complain about the interest charges right away because we thought we had made a mistake, but it just didn't sit well with us. We decided to call Chase on XX/XX/XXXX ( I think ) to complain about these charges and to ask for them to be refunded to us. When we called, one customer service agent told us that she couldn't file a complaint for us and that Chase always charged a daily interest rate on new purchases and that no balances were ever subject to a 30 day grace period ( which is customary for every credit card we've ever had ). Again, we were shocked by this information and didn't believe it was true, so we pulled out all of our past statements and saw that she was clearly incorrect- we had never been charged interest on any charges unless the statement had not been paid in full. We called back a second time that evening and was told that we were only charged interest after the balance transfer was completed because we were carrying a balance each month, despite the fact that that balance had a promotional 0 % interest period. She offered to refund us one of the interest fees in the amount of {$170.00}, but that felt like a drop in the bucket to us. We did not feel like the experience made us whole. 
We try to be diligent with our finances and read through our statements each month. The fact that we were confused by the interest charges and couldn't determine how and why they were being charged, and because this policy is clearly confusing to Chase 's own employees ( we heard three different policies from 5 different representatives ), we believe Chase 's terms are unclear and misleading. If we had understood that our terms would change because of the balance transfer ( either through the promotional wording or through their representatives ' explanations ), we would not have chosen to transfer the balance due to our use of the card on daily purchases.

complaint_what_happened:
Chase has placed two hard inquiries on my credit report for the same application that they are claiming are different now within a short period, which violates standard credit reporting practices.

Under FCRA ( 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ), creditors must ensure accurate reporting, and duplicate inquiries for a single application should not occur.

CFPB Regulation V ( 12 CFR 1022.42 ) requires creditors to report information fairly and accurately, yet Chase has failed to consolidate these inquiries.

FICO and VantageScore models are designed to deduplicate multiple inquiries within a set period ( typically 14-45 days ) to prevent unfair score penalties, yet Chase has disregarded this practice.

ECOA ( 12 CFR 1002.9 ) ensures fair lending practices, and generating multiple hard inquiries for the same application could be seen as unfair treatment.

Chase failed to properly handle inquiry deduplication under Metro 2 reporting standards, which require lenders to avoid multiple INQ hard inquiry codes for the same application. 
Pattern of Unfair and Deceptive Practices If Chase is systematically placing multiple inquiries on consumer credit reports without justification, this could be a violation of Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) under CFPB regulations. Repeated violations could lead to regulatory action, fines, or legal scrutiny.

Chases actions violate the principles of fair lending under the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) and the Consumer Financial Protection Act, which prohibit unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices. Defendant : JPMCB Card ( Chase ), a banking and credit services company headquartered in XXXX XXXX, NY, engaging in consumer credit reporting and debt collection activities across the United States.

Jurisdiction : This Court has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. 1331, as this case arises under federal statutes : the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( c ), and the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681.

FACTUAL BACKGROUND Cease Communication Request : On [ Date of Written Notification ], Plaintiff sent a written request to Chase, directing the Defendant to cease all communication regarding a disputed debt under the authority of 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( c ).

Continued Communication : Despite the clear written cease-communication request, Chase continued to attempt debt collection by contacting Plaintiff, violating FDCPA provisions under 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( c ).

Inaccurate Credit Reporting : JPMCB inaccurately reported Plaintiffs account status to credit bureaus, including [ XXXX, XXXX, XXXX ], by misrepresenting late payments and indicating an erroneous charge-off status. Despite Plaintiff disputing these inaccuracies with Chase and the credit bureaus, the errors remained uncorrected, resulting in negative marks on Plaintiffs credit. 
CLAIM I : VIOLATION OF THE FAIR DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES ACT, 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( c ) Elements Satisfied : Debt Collection Activity : Defendant, acting as a debt collector in this case, engaged in efforts to collect an alleged consumer debt from Plaintiff.

Cease-Communication Request : Plaintiff provided a valid, written cease-communication notice to Defendant, as per 15 U.S.C. 1692c ( c ).

Prohibited Communication : Defendant contacted Plaintiff after receiving the cease-communication request without meeting any permissible exceptions under the FDCPA.

Damages : Plaintiff suffered actual damages, including emotional distress and frustration, as a result of the unlawful communications. Plaintiff seeks statutory damages under 15 U.S.C. 1692k, as well as actual damages and reasonable attorneys fees.

CLAIM II : VIOLATION OF THE FAIR CREDIT REPORTING ACT, 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) AND 1681s-2 ( b ) Elements Satisfied : Inaccurate Reporting : Defendant inaccurately reported negative information on Plaintiffs credit report, including false late payment entries and an improper charge-off designation.

Failure to Investigate and Correct : Despite Plaintiffs disputes sent to both Defendant and the credit reporting agencies, Defendant did not conduct a reasonable investigation or correct the inaccuracies, violating 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ).

Damages : Defendants actions caused Plaintiff financial and emotional harm, resulting in a lower credit score and potential credit denials. Plaintiff seeks statutory damages, actual damages, punitive damages, and reasonable attorneys fees and costs.

RELIEF REQUESTED WHEREFORE, Plaintiff requests that this Court enter judgment in favor of Plaintiff and against Defendant as follows : a. Statutory damages under 15 U.S.C. 1692k ( a ) ( 2 ) ( A ) for FDCPA violations.

b. Actual damages for Plaintiffs emotional distress and financial harm.

c. Punitive damages under the FCRA for willful non-compliance. 
d. Reasonable attorneys fees and costs incurred in bringing this action. 
e. Any additional relief the Court deems just and proper.

In providing its services to a customer, a financial institution is required by law to exercise the care and skill of a diligent, prudent banker. Granted, there is room for diversity of view insofar as reasonableness is concerned. Indeed, there is a sense in which the standard of care of the reasonable person involves in its application a subjective element. 
However, it must be remembered that the correct test is always reasonable care in all circumstances, not average care. The fact that most people behave in a certain way may be good evidence that the conduct is reasonable, but this is not necessarily the case. Although reasonableness is a very fluid concept, all of the evidence suggests that JPMorgan Chase did not foresee the fraud and disregarded even the most obvious dangers in this respect.

The Core Issue with Interest Calculations The interest rate is the raw percentage charged on the amount I owe before any extra fees or calculations. The APR includes fees and represents the yearly cost of borrowing, while the Daily Periodic Rate ( DPR ) is just a small piece of the APR. But none of these numbers actually tell me the pure interest rate being used to calculate my charges, and thats a major issue.

APR is a long-term cost representation, DPR is just a step in the math, and the actual interest rate is the hidden percentage that controls how much Im truly being charged. Without knowing the true interest rate, there is no way to verify whether the lenders interest calculations are correct.

Here is a potential defense : Violation of Notification Requirements : Under the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), issuers must notify consumers of significant account changes, including closures, unless specific exceptions apply ( e.g., fraud or default ). If the closure was not due to such exceptions, the issuer may have violated TILA13. 

Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) Protections : If the closure impacted the clients credit report, the issuer must ensure accurate reporting. Any inaccuracies, such as implying default when none occurred, could constitute a breach of FCRA1. 

Unjustified Closure : The client had just activated the card and presumably had no chance to misuse it or violate terms. The issuer should provide a detailed explanation for the closure. complaint_what_happened:
On XX/XX/year> I deposited a check from my employer, XXXX XXXX, in the amount of {$6500.00}. At that time, Chase Bank placed a large deposit hold on the check, making the first {$220.00} of the check available immediately, and then {$5000.00} would be made available within two business days ( XX/XX/year> ), then the remainder would be made available after 7 business days. Mind you, the remitter of the check was the same as the remitter of my direct deposit to the same account. 

I had no issue with the large deposit hold, and scheduled payments accordingly. These were not big extravagant payments, rather they were my regular bills that I paid each month. My problem is that on XX/XX/year>, Chase Bank extended the hold on my deposit to 7 total business days. This was the day before my payments were scheduled to come out of my account and Chase subsequently returned 4 different payments. XXXX of which causing a returned payment fee of {$40.00} from my credit card issuer. 

Later that same week, I called the number on the hold notice provided to me to ask why the hold was extended. I wasn't provided any reasonable answer and was only told that they were allowed to do so because the check was large. I would disagree with that assessment. 

12 CFR 229.13 ( b ) clearly allowed for my deposit to be placed on a Large Deposit exception hold, however there was no relevant reason for Chase to extend the hold beyond that. I was not a new customer, I did not have a history of overdrafts, redeposited checks, and there were no emergency conditions. This tells me that Chase Bank extended the hold based on a " Reasonable cause to doubt collectability '' as prescribed under 12 CFR 229.13 ( e ). It even says as much on the hold notice that was sent to me after they decided to extend the hold. However, when I spoke to Chase about this during my phone call, not only could they not articulate any reason why they had a " reasonable doubt '', but the representative even told me that the only reason the hold was extended was because it was a large deposit and that it was unusual for me to deposit checks into my account. 

Now, I'm not an attorney, but Reg CC already has rules and provisions for placing a hold on a Large deposit. Chase blatantly chose to ignore those rules and provisions and extended the hold without a " Reasonable cause to doubt collectability, '' as defined in 12 CFR 229.13 ( e ) ( 1 ). To quote from the reg directly " Reasonable cause to believe a check is uncollectable requires the existence of facts that would cause a well-grounded belief in the mind of a reasonable person. '' Well, let me tell you the facts. The fact is that the check being deposited was from my employer, and the remitter on the check matched the name on my employer direct deposit that was deposited into the same Chase account every two weeks. Another fact is that the agent I spoke to told me the check was held due to it being a " large check. '' There are no other facts to this matter, and the check being " large '' is not a reason to have doubt that the check would not be paid. There was zero legitimate reasons to have " reasonable cause to doubt collectability. '' As a result of Chase 's practice to baselessly extend holds under the guise of " reasonable cause to doubt collectability, '' I, the consumer, have been harmed. And I would imagine other consumers have been harmed. As I previously stated, I made arrangements to pay certain bills after the Large Deposit hold was set to expire, and because the hold was baselessly extended, I had payments go unpaid and were returned with a fee.

JPMCB CARD SERVICES is in violation of the several CARD Act policies, and I would like to have this alleged account reviewed, modified or removed from my personal private consumer report. 
The following CARD Act violations apply : No interest rate increases for the first year. 
Credit card issuers generally can not raise interest rates, or any fees, during the first year an account is open, except when a variable rate changes, a promotional rate ends or a required minimum payment is more than 60 days late. 

Limits on fees and penalties. 
Over-limit fees. Cardholders can not be charged over-limit fees unless they give express permission ( opt in ) to the card issuer to approve transactions that exceed their credit limits. If permission is not given, transactions that exceed the credit limit most likely will be turned down. Without opt in card companies cant charge over-limit fees. I never gave express permission or opted in with JPMCB Card Services, but I was charged excessive fees. 

Double cycle billing. 
Although this act is prohibited, JPMCB Card Services included the previous billing period when calculating the amount of interest charged in the current billing cycle. 

Billing Statements. 
Delivery of statements. Credit card companies must mail ( or deliver electronically ) credit card bills at least 21 days before payment is due. If there is a grace period, the grace period must extend for at least a 21-day period from when the statement is mailed.

Also, Minimum payment warning. If you carry a balance, card companies must print on your billing statement the time and total interest it would take to pay off your current card balance if you only make minimum monthly payments. The bill must also disclose the monthly payment required to pay off the card balance in three years ( 36 months ). This is called the minimum payment warning, and it is designed to show cardholders how they can get out of debt more quickly by paying more than the minimum. The disclosure also must include a toll free number for credit counseling and debt management services. I was never afforded these requirements.

Finally, 15 USC 1666b ( a ) - Timing of payments.

A creditor may not treat a payment on a credit card account under an open end consumer credit plan as late for any purpose, unless the creditor has adopted reasonable procedures designed to ensure that each periodic statement including the information required by section 1637 ( b ) of this title is mailed or delivered to the consumer not later than 21 days before the payment due date.

In the CFPB comment for 1006.18 False, Deceptive, or Misleading Representations or Means : 18 ( e ) ( 1 ) Initial communications. 
1. Example. For example, assume that a debt collector who has not previously communicated with a consumer attempt to communicate with the consumer by leaving a limited-content message, as defined in 1006.2 ( j ). Pursuant to 1006.18 ( e ) ( 1 ), because the consumer-initiated call is the initial communication between the debt collector and the consumer, the debt collector must disclose to the consumer during that telephone call that the debt collector is attempting to collect a debt and that any information obtained will be used for that purpose.

Chase Bank offers a service call, " My Chase Plan '' for certain credit card charges. When signing up for this service there is information provided. Ultimately, the most egregious piece of information that is mislead and/or missing is : Chase allows consumers to apply additional payments to a credit card account that utilizes " My Chase Plan '' s, but Chase assumes the authority to allocate those funds across the different plans as it sees fit. Because this allocation is not defined by the terms and services, and Chases presumes that gives them the authority to dictate allocation, the methods of allocation can change at any time. Chase Bank can choose to allocate the funds to keep all of the plans at the same percent paid, ensuring you can not pay off any plan without pay off all plans simultaneously. 
When I called chase to make this payment, I was escalated to the highest available individual who confirmed, additional payments can be made, but not to a " My Chase Plan '' which the consumer dictates. Any additional payment will, as stated by this individual, be applied to the oldest plan. 
If a consumer has a " My Chase Plan '' with a low, or zero, monthly fee... the consumer may be required to pay off this plan before paying off a different plan. Again, this is not stipulated in the terms of service.

Subject : Complaint Against Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution for Violations of HJR 192, Public Law 73-10, UCC Provisions, Federal Regulations, U.S. Codes, and Unlawful Closure of Accounts Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ), I am filing this formal complaint against Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution for numerous violations of my rights, including but not limited to : failure to honor lawful payment instruments, improper retention of securities, violation of UCC and holder-in-due-course laws, breaches of federal regulations and U.S. Codes, unlawful closure of accounts, and potential theft, fraud, language fraud, and securities fraud. These actions contradict House Joint Resolution 192 ( HJR 192 ), Public Law 73-10 ( Emergency Banking Act ), the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ), the U.S. Constitution, and various federal laws and regulations.

Detailed Summary of Violations : Failure to Honor Securities and Lawful Payment Instruments : I tendered lawful payments using securities and negotiable instruments provided by Chase Bank, such as bills, statements, equity checks, bearer bonds, and coupons attached to the statements. According to UCC 3-104 ( a ) and UCC 3-302 ( a ) ( 2 ), these instruments are valid as negotiable instruments, and I accepted these securities " for value, '' issuing a restrictive endorsement as outlined in UCC 3-206. Additionally, I affixed postage stamps ( lawful money ) to these securities under HJR 192 and UCC 1-201 ( b ) ( 24 ), reinforcing my payments. Despite receiving these securities through registered and certified mail, Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution failed to discharge the debt, return the securities, or properly credit my account, in violation of UCC 3-603 ( b ).

This provision mandates that any obligation is discharged to the extent of a payment made by a negotiable instrument unless that instrument is returned or dishonored. Chase Bank 's retention of the securities without action violates my rights as both a creditor and holder of the instruments.

Unlawful Closure of Accounts and Definition of " Accounts '' : It is important to clarify that the term " account '' inherently means a place for deposits and withdrawals, not a static or limited financial agreement. As such, Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution unlawfully closed my accounts even after I had discharged the related debts through the lawful tender of securities. These accounts, by their nature, should be considered open-ended credit plans, which should not have a predetermined limit. Under my unlimited right to contract, as protected by the U.S. Constitution, I am entitled to maintain these accounts without arbitrary closure, particularly after meeting my financial obligations through lawful payments.

The attempt to impose artificial credit limits or close my accounts after the debt was discharged is unlawful. Setting limits on an open-ended credit plan, as Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution has done , is illegal and contrary to both the terms of open-ended credit and contract law principles. Their action constitutes a breach of UCC 3-311, concerning the resolution of debts through accord and satisfaction, and violates my constitutional right to contract freely without interference.

Potential Fraud, Theft, and Securities Fraud : In addition to their mishandling of the securities and failure to honor my lawful payments, I am concerned that Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution may be engaging in fraudulent activities.

By retaining the securities I sent, continuing to demand payment for already discharged debts, and unlawfully closing accounts, they may be guilty of theft, securities fraud, and other forms of financial fraud. Their refusal to properly process the negotiable instruments and their subsequent closure of the accounts indicate potential securities fraud under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and related provisions under federal securities laws. Language fraud may also be present in the manner in which the terms of my accounts, securities, and payments have been communicated. Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution has used deceptive or unclear language that obscures the nature of my rights and obligations, particularly in regard to the use of lawful money and the nature of the securities provided. By misleading me about the status of the accounts and payments, they are potentially engaging in fraudulent misrepresentation under 18 U.S. Code 1341 ( Mail Fraud ) and 18 U.S. Code 1343 ( Wire Fraud ).

Violation of Holder-in-Due-Course Laws : As the holder of the securities and negotiable instruments I tendered, I am entitled to the protections and rights outlined in UCC 3-302. A holder in due course has the right to enforce the payment of the instrument free from most claims and defenses. Chase Bank, by refusing to honor my position as the holder of these instruments, has violated my holder-in-due-course rights. They retained the securities without processing them, have continued to unlawfully demand further payments, and have denied my rightful claim to the value of these instruments, in violation of UCC 3-305 ( concerning defenses and claims to an instrument ).

Violation of U.S. Codes and Federal Regulations : By refusing to process the private instruments I provided, unlawfully retaining my securities, and denying my right to claim them, Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution has violated various U.S. codes , including 12 U.S. Code 411, which governs the issuance and use of lawful money. Additionally, they have breached multiple provisions of the Code of Federal Regulations ( CFR ), particularly those governing the handling of negotiable instruments and securities. The improper handling of these private instruments suggests potential violations of 15 U.S. Code Chapter 41- Consumer Credit Protection.

Failure to Discharge Debt Under the Emergency Banking Act and Gold Clause : According to Public Law 73-10 ( Emergency Banking Act ) and HJR 192, all debts must be discharged upon the tender of lawful money. My payment, which consisted of securities and lawful money ( postage stamps ), fully satisfied the obligation. Chase Bank Credit/Banking Institution has unlawfully refused to recognize the discharge of my debt, in violation of the Gold Clause, which prohibits the refusal to accept lawful money for the satisfaction of debts. Their continued claims that I owe further payments after I have already tendered lawful payment indicate a violation of both public law and federal monetary statutes.

Applicable UCC, Federal Regulations, U.S. Codes, and Constitutional Protections : UCC 3-104 ( a ) : Defines a negotiable instrument as an unconditional promise or order to pay a fixed amount of money.

UCC 3-206 : Governs restrictive endorsements and their legal effect on the instrument.

UCC 3-302 : Holder-in-due-course rights and their protection in the enforcement of negotiable instruments.

UCC 3-305 : Outlines claims and defenses to negotiable instruments, including wrongful retention.

UCC 3-311 : Covers accord and satisfaction, requiring that when a debt is discharged, no further payment can be demanded.

UCC 3-603 ( b ) : States that an obligation is discharged to the extent of any payment made by a negotiable instrument unless it is returned or dishonored.

UCC 1-201 ( b ) ( 24 ) : Defines lawful money, including postage stamps affixed to negotiable instruments.

12 U.S. Code 411 : Governs the issuance and receipt of lawful money and its proper application in discharging debts.

18 U.S. Code 1341 ( Mail Fraud ) : Prohibits the use of mail to execute fraudulent schemes.

Shortly after I reported the fraudulent activity, Chase unexpectedly closed my credit card account without prior notice or explanation. This decision penalized me for reporting fraudulent activity and violated several consumer protection laws.

First, under the Fair Credit Billing Act ( FCBA ), consumers have the right to dispute fraudulent charges without facing penalties. Chases decision to close my account directly violated 15 U.S.C. 1666, which prohibits any negative consequences resulting from a valid dispute over billing errors or fraud. Similarly, 15 U.S.C. 1666i stipulates that actions such as account closures should not affect a consumers creditworthiness or result in penalties after disputing fraudulent activity. By closing my account, Chase failed to uphold these protections.

Second, Chase violated the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), specifically 15 U.S.C. 1641 ( g ), which requires creditors to provide clear and prior written notice of any material changes to a credit account, such as closures. Chase did not provide such notice or explain the rationale for the closure, depriving me of the transparency required by law.

Third, Chases actions also breached the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( ECOA ), outlined in 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( a ), which ensures that consumers are not discriminated against for exercising their rights under consumer protection laws. By closing my account after I reported fraud, Chase penalized me for taking appropriate steps to dispute unauthorized charges, which constitutes a discriminatory and retaliatory action.

Finally, Chases failure to handle this issue appropriately also contravenes CFPB regulations under 12 C.F.R. 1026.13, which state that consumers disputing billing errors or fraudulent charges should not face adverse consequences like account closures or penalties.

In response, I sent a detailed letter to Chase outlining these violations and requesting the immediate reinstatement of my account and removal of any adverse credit reports related to the fraudulent charges. The reason for my complaint is that although buried in the terms for opting to use the Pay Over Time option for a large purchase is the fact that all payments over and above the calculated Interest Savings Balance are first credited against the Pay Over Time Account, this is a deceptive practice. The math for calculating the Interest Savings Balance is the following : Monthly Payment = Monthly Purchases - Pay Over Time Balance + Monthly Pay Over Time Payment. In my case I had expected a payment of approximately {$3500.00}. However, when I received my statement, my payment was approximately {$6000.00}. After studying my statement I determined the following : XXXX. I purchase a refundable XXXX ticket for {$2500.00}. 
XXXX. I could not fly as scheduled so I cancelled my flight and received a refund from XXXX in the amount of {$2500.00}. 
Chase did the following ; My Monthly Purchase included the {$2500.00} XXXX ticket. The Pay Over Time Balance was reduced by {$2500.00}, thus increasing my payment by {$2500.00}. As you can see, I purchased nothing and Chase paid out nothing, yet Chase ends up with an additional {$2500.00} this month, and the value of the Pay Over Time option was negated. 

Chase told me I should have arranged with XXXX to have the refund paid to me in some other form to avoid having my Pay Over Time balance reduced.

I was able to use other funds to pay this unexpected amount, but I am sure many people are not. This deceptive practice essentially enables Chase to move customers from the advantageous Pay Over Time option into paying the huge current interest amounts of 19.49 % on monthly outstanding credit card balances.

I see all cards now pushing this Pay Over Time concept. The reason is obvious, the card companies understand that they can use this concept to move people into paying high interest rates on outstanding balances. CFPB should move to prevent this deceptive practice and put the Pay Over Time balance onto a level playing field for customers.

1026.11 Treatment of credit balances ; account termination. 
( a ) Credit balances. When a credit balance in excess of {$1.00} is created on a credit account ( through transmittal of funds to a creditor in excess of the total balance due on an account, through rebates of unearned finance charges or insurance premiums, or through amounts otherwise owed to or held for the benefit of the consumer ), the creditor shall : ( 1 ) Credit the amount of the credit balance to the consumer 's account ; ( 2 ) Refund any part of the remaining credit balance within seven business days from receipt of a written request from the consumer ; ( 3 ) Make a good faith effort to refund to the consumer by cash, check, or money order, or credit to a deposit account of the consumer, any part of the credit balance remaining in the account for more than six months. No further action is required if the consumer 's current location is not known to the creditor and can not be traced through the consumer 's last known address or telephone number.

( b ) Account termination.

( 1 ) A creditor shall not terminate an account prior to its expiration date solely because the consumer does not incur a finance charge.

( 2 ) Nothing in paragraph ( b ) ( 1 ) of this section prohibits a creditor from terminating an account that is inactive for three or more consecutive months. An account is inactive for purposes of this paragraph if no credit has been extended ( such as by purchase, cash advance or balance transfer ) and if the account has no outstanding balance. 

( c ) Timely settlement of estate debts ( XXXX ) General rule. 

( i ) Reasonable policies and procedures required. ( ii ) Application to joint accounts. Paragraph ( c ) of this section does not apply to the account of a deceased consumer if a joint accountholder remains on the account.

( 2 ) Timely statement of balance ( i ) Requirement. Upon request by the administrator of an estate, a card issuer must provide the administrator with the amount of the balance on a deceased consumer 's account in a timely manner.

( ii ) Safe harbor. For purposes of paragraph ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) of this section, providing the amount of the balance on the account within 30 days of receiving the request is deemed to be timely.

The checks were made payable to me ( as the attorney ), my client, and his wife ( over XXXX XXXX  ). My client is also my brother. All three of us endorsed the checks before deposit. 

Initially, I was informed that the funds would be available on XX/XX/year>, and XX/XX/year>. However, on XX/XX/XXXX, I was told the release date had changed to XX/XX/year>. Then, on XX/XX/XXXX, I received a text message stating that a restriction had been placed on my account and that I needed to call to resolve the issue. 

I spoke with a representative from the fraud department, who advised that Chase l needed to verify that the listed payee endorsed the check. He requested phone numbers for the other two listed payees, which I provided. When he entered their numbers into the Chase system he stated that the numbers came back verified/registered under different names so Chase could not call them to verify the endorsements. We discussed other methods of verification and the representative acknowledged that Chase had usually strict policies that did not make sense but he had to do his job. I then requested to speak with a supervisor. 

I then spoke with the supervisor he was immediately rude and unprofessional. He asked several questions about my XXXX XXXX and looked up my credentials on the bar websites for Kentucky and Georgia. He confirmed that I am an XXXX  in good standing in both jurisdictions. He then asked whether I was related to one of the payees, as we share the same last name. I confirmed that he is my brother. The supervisor then reiterated that Chase needed to verify that the payees had actually signed the checks and again requested their phone numbers. After providing their numbers, I was again informed that the system did not verify the numbers as belonging to the listed payees.

I found this confusing, as the number provided was my clients personal mobile number registered with XXXX XXXX The representative stated that the account and funds would remain on hold until verification could be completed. I asked whether other forms of verificationsuch as providing a drivers license or visiting a branch in personcould be used, but he rudely responded by saying that if there were other alternative methods he would have said so. I requested to speak with a manager and informed him that I would visit a branch the following day. The conversation with this supervisor was so unhelpful and unpleasant. Extremely disheartening to be spoken to in this manner After speaking with my client, I obtained a copy of his phone bill showing that the number is registered to him under his personal account. He also contacted XXXX, which confirmed that their system lists the number under his name. 

On XX/XX/year>, I visited my local Chase branch to resolve the issue. The branch agent contacted multiple representatives from the back office and fraud department, all of whom reiterated that the only verification method was through the phone number. However, they said a manager would follow up. 


While at the branch, I had my client on the phone as he contacted XXXX again. The XXXX representative conducted another system check, performed a reset, and had a technician verify that my clients number was correctly registered under his name across all their systems. 

Additionally, while I was at the branch, my client called the local branch multiple times, and his name appeared on the agents caller ID. 

We waited a few hours to see if the reset performed by XXXX XXXX update my clients name in Chases system. I then contacted the Chase fraud department again and this time with my client on the phone. We explained the situation to the representative and she checked his number in their system but it was still showing as verified under a different name. We again asked for other verification methods and she refused to allow any other means of verification. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, the funds were marked as available in my account, yet I remained unable to access them due to the restriction. I called the fraud department again and requested that they reattempt verification using my clients number. The representative stated that, in their system, my clients number was linked to a different individual. I explained the situation and referenced the documentation provided, but the representative refused to accept any alternative form of verification. 

I once again requested that the issue be escalated and that I speak with a manager. As of now, my account and funds remain on hold. Chase has advised that they can continue to hold my funds and that, after a certain period, they may close my account.

The verification process imposed by Chase is excessively rigid and unreasonably restrictive, effectively creating an insurmountable barrier for legitimate account holders to verify their own transactions. Despite multiple efforts to provide alternative forms of proofthe bank refused to consider any alternative means of authentication beyond its flawed internal phone number verification system. 

This process fails to account for common and legitimate circumstances, such as mobile carriers not always reflecting real-time name updates in third-party databases, family members sharing last names, or the fact that caller ID and official phone bills clearly establish ownership of a number. By refusing to accept any other form of verificationChase has created a process that is not only impractical but also virtually impossible to satisfy. 

As a result, even fully compliant customers with transparent, lawful transactions are left without access to their own funds, facing unnecessary delays and financial hardship due to a system that prioritizes rigid bureaucracy over reasonable, good-faith verification.

The Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) is a federal law that regulates how consumer credit information is collected, disseminated, and used. It aims to ensure accuracy, fairness, and privacy of information in the files of consumer reporting agencies. Here are some key points regarding inaccuracies and reporting violations under the FCRA : # # # Inaccuracies Under the FCRA 1. **Consumer Rights** : Consumers have the right to dispute inaccurate or incomplete information in their credit reports. If a consumer identifies an error, they can file a dispute with the credit reporting agency ( CRA ).

2. **Investigation Requirement** : Upon receiving a dispute, the CRA must investigate the claim, usually within 30 days. They must review the information provided by the consumer and verify the accuracy of the disputed information with the original source.

3. **Correction of Errors** : If the investigation finds that the information is indeed inaccurate, the CRA must correct or delete the information from the consumer 's credit report.

4. **Notification** : If a correction is made, the CRA must notify the consumer and provide them with a free copy of their credit report, which reflects the changes.

5. **Reinsertion of Information** : If the CRA later re-inserts the disputed information, they must notify the consumer within five business days.

# # # Reporting Violations 1. **Failure to Investigate** : If a CRA fails to conduct a reasonable investigation of a dispute, it may be in violation of the FCRA.

2. **Inaccurate Reporting** : Reporting inaccurate information, even if it was not done intentionally, can lead to violations. CRAs and furnishers ( entities that provide information to CRAs ) are responsible for ensuring the accuracy of the information they report.

3. **Failure to Provide Required Disclosures** : The FCRA requires CRAs to provide certain disclosures to consumers, including the right to dispute information. Failure to provide these disclosures can be a violation.

4. **Negligence and Willful Noncompliance** : If a CRA or furnisher knowingly reports inaccurate information or fails to comply with the FCRA, they may be liable for damages. Consumers can sue for actual damages, statutory damages, and in some cases, punitive damages.

5. **Consumer Reporting Agencies** : The FCRA applies not only to CRAs but also to entities that furnish information to CRAs. These furnishers must ensure that the information they provide is accurate and up-to-date.

Chase has been and is currently treating payments on my credit card account under my open end consumer credit plan as late without utilizing reasonable procedures designed to ensure that each periodic statement including the information required by 15 U.S.C. 1637 of the Truth In Lending Act ( TILA ) was delivered to me before the payment due date. Also, Chase has failed to meet additional requirements contained in the regulations prescribed by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) which are designed to carry out the purposes of the TILA.

15 U.S.C. 1637 ( i ) mandates that a creditor must provide written notice of any significant change in terms, as defined by the CFPBs rules, at least 45 days before the change takes effect. 12 CFR 1026.9 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( ii ) specifies that a " significant change in account terms '' includes an increase in the required minimum periodic payment. Accordingly, 12 CFR 1026.9 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( i ) ( A ) requires a creditor to deliver written notice of such changes at least 45 days prior to the effective date to each affected consumer. Further, 12 CFR 1026.9 ( c ) ( 2 ) ( iv ) mandates that this advance notice must include specific information, including but not limited to, the amount of any increase in the required minimum periodic payment, a statement that account terms are being changed, the effective date of these changes, and adherence to prescribed format requirements for such notices.

Legal implications arise from Chases non-compliance with TILAs requirements, potentially triggering both civil and criminal liability. These repeated violations not only undermine the regulatory framework established by the Truth in Lending Act but also have directly damaged my financial standing. Chases failure to provide the required 45-day notices for significant changes to my account terms has resulted in inaccurate and unfair reporting of late payments, ultimately harming my creditworthiness and limiting my access to fair financial opportunities. By neglecting their obligation to implement reasonable procedures and timely notifications, Chase has compromised the protections intended by Congress to safeguard consumers from precisely this kind of financial harm and instability.

The Truth in Lending Act mandates these disclosures to prevent unjust financial impacts and assure consumers are not misled or unfairly penalized. complaint_what_happened:
I am filing a formal complaint against JPMCB Card Services ( hereinafter referred to as " the creditor '' ) for violations of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) and improper credit reporting practices. 

Upon reviewing my credit report, I have identified multiple instances of inaccurate and potentially unlawful reporting by this creditor regarding a charged-off account ( Account Number : XXXX ). The details of the violations are as follows : 1. Repeated Charge-Off Reporting ( FCRA Violation 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) ) The creditor has been reporting a new charge-off every single month, as evidenced in my XXXX payment history on my credit report. 
A charge-off is a single event, not a recurring one. Repeatedly reporting it re-ages the debt, misleading lenders and unfairly lowering my credit score.

This practice falsely extends the delinquency period and violates the accuracy and fairness provisions under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ).

2. Inaccurate Balance & Past Due Reporting ( FCRA Violation 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( B ) ) The creditor reported a charge-off amount of {$1100.00} while simultaneously reporting a past due amount of {$1000.00}.

A charged-off account should not continue to accrue past-due balances unless it is actively being billed, which is not the case here. 
This reporting contradicts itself and misleads credit reporting agencies, violating the FCRAs requirement for accurate reporting. 
3. Failure to Properly Update Account Status ( FCRA Violation 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 2 ) ) If an account is charged-off, the balance should be " XXXX past due '' unless the creditor is still billing me, which they are not. 
The status update in XX/XX/XXXX should have reflected the charge-off as a one-time event, yet it continues to be reported monthly in XXXX and now into XXXX. 
4. Possible Re-Aging of the Debt ( FCRA Violation 1681c ( a ) ( 4 ) ) The original delinquency date appears to have been altered or not clearly stated. Under 15 U.S.C. 1681c ( a ) ( 4 ), a negative item should only remain on a credit report for XXXX years from the original delinquency date. 
By repeatedly reporting charge-offs, it appears that the creditor is re-aging the account, which is illegal under the FCRA. 

I respectfully request that the CFPB investigate this matter and ensure that JPMCB Card Services corrects these violations. Specifically, I request : Immediate removal of this account from my credit reports from all 3 bureaus due to repeated and inaccurate reporting.

Assurance that JPMCB will comply with FCRA regulations in future reporting practices. 
If this matter is not resolved promptly, I will be left with no choice but to escalate this complaint by filing a formal dispute with my states Attorney General.

d to consumer reporting agencies are not only factually inaccurate but also legally unenforceable, based on violations of the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) and the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ).

1. Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1666b Failure to Provide Minimum Grace Period for Payment Under 15 U.S.C. 1666b, creditors must ensure that any credit card statement reflecting a balance is sent at least 21 days before the payment due date. If the statement was not delivered within this window, any late fee assessment or negative credit reporting tied to that statement may be unlawful.

It is unclear whether the required statement timing standard was met in the billing cycles associated with the reported late payments. If the creditor failed to comply with the minimum 21-day advance notice requirement, any related delinquency reporting is legally defective and should be deleted immediately.

2. Upon receiving a proper dispute, the creditor must : Acknowledge the dispute within 30 days, and Resolve or investigate it within 90 days ( or two billing cycles ).

If the creditor failed to properly respond to any disputes I raised in writing concerning incorrect due dates, misapplied payments, or system errors, then continued reporting of a late payment is in violation of Regulation Z and must be removed.

3. Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) Obligation to Report Accurate Information As required by 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), any information furnished to a consumer reporting agency must be complete and accurate. This statutory obligation includes late payment reporting.

I also saw deductions of these payments from my checking account, but again, the payees were not specified. As a result, I had no actual notice of fraudulent payment of these checks at this point.

The altered checks were in the same dollar amounts I had written to the IRS and GA Dept of Revenue, but they were made to individuals I do not know. I immediately presented to a Chase branch that same day and made a fraud claim. 

The following day on XX/XX/XXXX, I met with an XXXX Police Department officer at the mailbox where I had dropped off these checks, and a police report was made. I also called the United States Postal Inspection Service to report the incident. I then returned to Chase to fill out a Declaration of Unauthorized Endorsement and Altered Item form per their instructions. On XX/XX/XXXX, I received notice via phone call from Chase that my claim had been declined due to not making the claim within 30 days of the fraudulent payment. Issue : Rewards Redemption Deceptive or Misleading Practices Company : JPMorgan Chase Bank , N.A . 

Complaint : Im filing this complaint regarding my experience with Chase related to redeeming my Ultimate Rewards points via direct deposit. 

As a Chase/XXXX  XXXX XXXX, I attempted to redeem my rewards points as a direct deposit to an external bank account. The Chase website clearly states that you can go to " Profile and Settings '' to add an external account for direct deposit of rewards. However, this option does not exist anywhere in the interface.

Even after doing this, the external account did not appear as an option for depositing rewards.

This process should be simple and straightforward, but Chase has made it unnecessarily convoluted, and it feels intentionally designed to discourage direct deposit redemptions in favor of statement credit which results in more profit for the company. This made submitting any thoughtful or clearly written complaint nearly impossible, further reinforcing the impression that Chase is actively trying to prevent users from voicing concerns or holding them accountable.

In short, I believe Chase is engaging in deceptive practices by : Advertising a feature ( adding an external account via Profile and Settings for rewards ) that does not exist Making the process to redeem points as direct deposit intentionally difficult Designing a feedback system that discourages clear communication by rejecting standard punctuation I am seriously considering closing my account over this experience. I am requesting that the CFPB review this issue and push Chase to ( 1 ) correct its misleading documentation, ( 2 ) make direct deposit redemption of rewards truly accessible, and ( 3 ) provide a basic, usable way for customers to submit feedback.

Under the Privacy act of 1974, I have the right to be protected against unwarranted invasion of their privacy resulting from the collection, maintenance, use, and disclosure of their personal information. 


15 U.S. Code 1681- Congressional findings and statement of purpose ( a ) Accuracy and fairness of credit reporting The Congress makes the following findings : ( 1 ) The banking system is dependent upon fair and accurate credit reporting. Inaccurate credit reports directly impair the efficiency of the banking system, and unfair credit reporting methods undermine the public confidence which is essential to the continued functioning of the banking system.

( 2 ) An elaborate mechanism has been developed for investigating and evaluating the credit worthiness, credit standing, credit capacity, character, and general reputation of consumers.

( 3 ) Consumer reporting agencies have assumed a vital role in assembling and evaluating consumer credit and other information on consumers.

( 4 ) There is a need to insure that consumer reporting agencies exercise their grave responsibilities with fairness, impartiality, and a respect for the consumers right to privacy. 
( b ) Reasonable procedures It is the purpose of this subchapter to require that consumer reporting agencies adopt reasonable procedures for meeting the needs of commerce for consumer credit, personnel, insurance, and other information in a manner which is fair and equitable to the consumer, with regard to the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy, and proper utilization of such information in accordance with the requirements of this subchapter. 

( Pub. L. 90321, title VI, 602, as added Pub. L. 91508, title VI, 601, Oct. 26, 1970, 84 Stat. 1128. ) 15 U.S. Code 6802 - Obligations with respect to disclosures of personal information ( a ) Notice requirements Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, a financial institution XXXX not, directly or through any affiliate, disclose to a nonaffiliated third party any nonpublic personal information, unless such financial institution provides or has provided to the consumer a notice that complies with section 6803 of this title.

( b ) Opt out ( 1 ) In general A financial institution may not disclose nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party unless ( A ) such financial institution clearly and conspicuously discloses to the consumer, in writing or in electronic form or other form permitted by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title, that such information may be disclosed to such third party ; ( B ) the consumer is given the opportunity, before the time that such information is initially disclosed, to direct that such information not be disclosed to such third party ; and ( C ) the consumer is given an explanation of how the consumer can exercise that nondisclosure option.

( 2 ) Exception This subsection shall not prevent a financial institution from providing nonpublic personal information to a nonaffiliated third party to perform services for or functions on behalf of the financial institution, including marketing of the financial institutions own products or services, or financial products or services offered pursuant to joint agreements between two or more financial institutions that comply with the requirements imposed by the regulations prescribed under section 6804 of this title, if the financial institution fully discloses the providing of such information and enters into a contractual agreement with the third party that requires the third party to maintain the confidentiality of such information. 

( c ) Limits on reuse of information Except as otherwise provided in this subchapter, a nonaffiliated third party that receives from a financial institution nonpublic personal information under this section shall not, directly or through an affiliate of such receiving third party, disclose such information to any other person that is a nonaffiliated third party of both the financial institution and such receiving third party, unless such disclosure would be lawful if made directly to such other person by the financial institution. 

( d ) Limitations on the sharing of account number information for marketing purposes A financial institution shall not disclose, other than to a consumer reporting agency, an account number or similar form of access number or access code for a credit card account, deposit account, or transaction account of a consumer to any nonaffiliated third party for use in telemarketing, direct mail marketing, or other marketing through electronic mail to the consumer. 

( e ) General exceptions Subsections ( a ) and ( b ) shall not prohibit the disclosure of nonpublic personal information ( 1 ) as necessary to effect, administer, or enforce a transaction requested or authorized by the consumer, or in connection with ( A ) servicing or processing a financial product or service requested or authorized by the consumer ; ( B ) maintaining or servicing the consumers account with the financial institution, or with another entity as part of a private label credit card program or other extension of credit on behalf of such entity ; or ( C ) a proposed or actual securitization, secondary market sale ( including sales of servicing rights ), or similar transaction related to a transaction of the consumer ; ( 2 ) with the consent or at the direction of the consumer ; ( 3 ) ( A ) to protect the confidentiality or security of the financial institutions records pertaining to the consumer, the service or product, or the transaction therein ; ( B ) to protect against or prevent actual or potential fraud, unauthorized transactions, claims, or other liability ; ( C ) for required institutional risk control, or for resolving customer disputes or inquiries ; ( D ) to persons holding a legal or beneficial interest relating to the consumer ; or ( E ) to persons acting in a fiduciary or representative capacity on behalf of the consumer ; ( 4 ) to provide information to insurance rate advisory organizations, guaranty funds or agencies, applicable rating agencies of the financial institution, persons assessing the institutions compliance with industry standards, and the institutions attorneys, accountants, and auditors ; ( 5 ) to the extent specifically permitted or required under other provisions of law and in accordance with the Right to Financial Privacy Act of 1978 [ 12 U.S.C. 3401 et seq. ], to law enforcement agencies ( including the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection [ 1 ] a Federal functional regulator, the Secretary of the Treasury with respect to subchapter II of chapter 53 of title 31, and chapter 2 of title I of Public Law 91508 ( 12 U.S.C. 19511959 ), a State insurance authority, or the Federal Trade Commission ), self-regulatory organizations, or for an investigation on a matter related to public safety ; ( 6 ) ( A ) to a consumer reporting agency in accordance with the Fair Credit Reporting Act [ 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq. ], or ( B ) from a consumer report reported by a consumer reporting agency ; ( 7 ) in connection with a proposed or actual sale, merger, transfer, or exchange of all or a portion of a business or operating unit if the disclosure of nonpublic personal information concerns solely consumers of such business or unit; or ( 8 ) to comply with Federal, State, or local laws, rules, and other applicable legal requirements ; to comply with a properly authorized civil, criminal, or regulatory investigation or subpoena or summons by Federal, State, or local authorities ; or to respond to judicial process or government regulatory authorities having jurisdiction over the financial institution for examination, compliance, or other purposes as authorized by law.

( " Chase '' ) for unlawful and deceptive practices concerning the closure of both my personal and business credit card accounts without cause or explanation, continued interest accrual post-closure, improper collection efforts, and violations of federal law regarding account receivables and securitization processes.Allegations:1. Improper Interest Charges Post-Account Closure : Chase continued to charge interest on my personal and business credit card accounts after they were unilaterally closed by the bank, despite my lack of access to further credit and usage. This violates basic contract principles and constitutes an unjust enrichment.Supporting Case Law : See Koerner v. CitiMortgage, Inc., 912 F. Supp. 2d 1207 ( D. Minn. 2012 ), which states that continued interest accrual after contract termination, without legal authority or performance, can constitute breach of good faith and fair dealing.2. Failure to Apply Offsets from Sale of Receivables Violation of 15 U.S.C. 1666h : Chase sold the credit card account receivables to third parties for securitization into asset-backed securities ( ABS ), deriving funds from this sale. Under 15 U.S.C. 1666h, a creditor shall not take any action to collect any amount of a credit transaction which the consumer has disputed, particularly when that amount has been satisfied or offset by the sale or assignment of the receivable.Statute Reference:15 U.S. Code 1666h ( b ) If a creditor sells or assigns a debt that is the subject of a billing dispute to a third party ... the consumers rights under this section shall remain in effect.Legal Principle : Proceeds from the sale of consumer receivablesespecially when securitizedmust be used to satisfy or offset the original obligation.3. Double Recovery ( Double Dipping ) through Collection on Satisfied Debt : After selling the receivable, Chase continued to collect payments from me, effectively engaging in double recovery, which constitutes unjust enrichment, fraudulent concealment, and bad faith under UCC principles.Case Law : In re Smith, 737 F.2d 1549 ( 11th Cir. 1984 ) A creditor may not recover more than the amount owed, and attempts to collect on discharged or satisfied debts are unlawful.Restatement ( Third ) of Restitution and Unjust Enrichment 1 A person who has been unjustly enriched at the expense of another is subject to liability in restitution.4. Failure to Disclose True Creditor Relationship and Nature of the Promissory Note UCC Article 3 : My signature on the original credit application created a negotiable instrument under UCC 3-104, which Chase used to originate credit by depositing it into a Special Purpose Vehicle ( SPV ) trust or conduit entity. Chase failed to disclose that my signed instrument constituted the originating asset and that they acted solely as an intermediary, not a lender.UCC References : UCC 3-104 Definition of a negotiable instrument, which includes a signed, unconditional promise to pay.UCC 3-105 ( a ) The note becomes an instrument once issued and transferred into the commercial stream.UCC 9-203 and 9-309 Address attachment and perfection of security interests through the creation and assignment of financial instruments.5. Failure to Provide Truthful Disclosures Under TILA and FDCPA : Chase failed to disclose the true nature of the transaction, the securitization of the receivables, and the resulting third-party ownership, in violation of the Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ) and the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ). Statutes Involved:15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq. TILA requires full disclosure of the terms of credit and the parties involved.15 U.S.C . 1692e FDCPA prohibits deceptive or misleading representations in connection with the collection of any debt.

Exception holds are used for accounts that have been frequently overdrawn, or when banks have reason to suspect that a deposit is legitimate. Under accounting and legal standards, a charge-off is a one-time event. Repeated reporting of this charge-off constitutes inaccurate reporting and violates FCRA Section 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) ( 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ) ), which requires furnishers to provide accurate and complete information. 
This inaccurate reporting is also in violation of FCRA Section 607 ( b ) ( 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ) ), which mandates that furnishers must adopt procedures that ensure the maximum possible accuracy of consumer information. By continuing to report the charge-off on a monthly basis, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX Bank, Jp Morgan Chase XXXX XXXX XXXX BaXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX has fraudulently extended the negative impact of this event on my credit score.

Reporting a credit limit falsely suggests that there is still available credit, which affects my credit utilization ratio and further damages my credit score. This practice is in clear violation of the accuracy standards required under 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ), as the information furnished is neither relevant nor accurate.

This principle applies here because [ Creditors Name ] can not continue reporting and benefiting from the charge-off while the debt has been discharged or sold. 
XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  : The Tax Court ruled that once a debt is claimed as uncollectible, it can not be treated as still owed. By continuing to report the accountXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Jp Morgan Chase, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  are attempting to assert the existence of a debt that has already been deemed worthless. 
XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX v. XXXX, XXXX XXXX. XXXX ( XXXX ) : This case reinforces that a creditor can not claim a bad debt deduction while simultaneously attempting to assert the debts collectibility.
